newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan epidemic, firm prices may spur pork imports.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan epidemic, firm prices may spur pork imports.

text.p: Taiwan's pork imports may rise in the third quarter as a seven-week-old farm epidemic squeezes supplies for what until late March was a major pork exporter, officials said on Monday.

Pork prices, which collapsed after the cabinet's Council of Agriculture announced an outbreak of hog foot and mouth disease on March 20, have fully rebounded as the mandatory slaughter of all pigs at affected farms slashed supplies.
"The massive loss of pigs will cut pork supplies deep in the third quarter and provides opportunities for pork importers," Council of Agriculture official Liao An-ting told Reuters.
Liao declined to estimate Taiwan's 1997 pork imports.
Taiwan has slaughtered millions of pigs since March 20, when the farm council banned pork exports and ordered all pigs, even healthy ones, destroyed at all infected farms.

Council data showed the deadly virus had been detected on 5,501 of Taiwan's 25,000 hog farms, with official projections showing that 4.39 million of the island's 14 million pigs have been or would have to be destroyed.

Pork prices initially fell by more than 60 percent, but the slaughter now has sharply reduced supplies. Wholesale prices had recovered by Monday to levels not seen since before the outbreak at T$44-T$50 (US$1.6-$1.8) per kg.
One industry analyst predicted Taiwan's farms would need six months to reproduce enough pigs to stabilise supply and demand, and that would not help alleviate third-quarter shortages.
"October would be the earliest for hog herds to return to healthy levels," he said.
In 1996, Taiwan exported about 271,000 tonnes of pork, mainly to Japan, which banned imports from Taiwan after the epidemic broke out to ensure the safety of its own herds.
Taiwan imported some 11,000 tonnes from the United States in 1996, farm officials said.
Analysts said Taiwan, under pressure to open more markets, was most likely to source any potential pork imports from U.S. producers.
U.S. and Canadian pork producers have urged Taiwan to open its markets for more pork imports by lifting import bans on hog stomachs, feet, tongues and other pork cuts.

The farm council announced last Thursday that the epidemic appeared to have been controlled, as only 19 new cases were reported on Wednesday. Subsequent council figures showed only six new cases were found on Sunday.
